title: Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016
short_title: Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would give around 10,000 eligible people a larger one-off payment under an existing scheme and make related changes to how the scheme is run.
The payment would rise from half to 70 per cent of the gap between what a person was actually paid and what they would have been paid using only the productivity part of the assessment tool.
People who already received a payment would get a top-up automatically, and the requirement to get legal advice before payment would become optional instead of mandatory.
changes: Increases the payment rate from 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the wage difference.
Makes the requirement to obtain legal advice voluntary rather than compulsory.
Extends all relevant payment scheme dates by 12 months to give people more time to register and apply.
summary.affected: Around 10,000 eligible people who were employed and assessed using the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool, including those who have already received a payment under the scheme.

speeches.speaker: Jenny Macklin
speeches.brief: The bill amends the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme to increase back pay for people with disability from 50% to 70% of the wage difference, implementing a settlement reached after a class action. The speaker also urges the government to finalise a new non-discriminatory wage assessment tool and address funding shortfalls for Australian disability enterprises.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016, which provides 70% back pay to workers with intellectual disability underpaid due to a discriminatory wage assessment tool, and called it an improvement over a prior 50% offer from the Abbott-Turnbull government, respecting claimants' wishes and the class action settlement.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: The speaker welcomed the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016, which provides 70% compensation to supported employees underpaid via the discriminatory BSWAT, and urged the government to finalise a new non-discriminatory wage tool. They highlighted local disability enterprises like Radius Disability Services and Bendigo Access Employment, and raised concerns about the tool's misuse, such as a Bendigo traffic management business underpaying workers at $2 an hour to win contracts.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The member supported the bill, which implements a settlement raising compensation for supported wage employees to 70% of their alleged loss, up from 50% under the 2014 legislation, with automatic top-up payments for those already paid. The member also noted the unresolved discriminatory BSWAT tool is being addressed through Fair Work Australia conciliation before Deputy President Anna Booth, and defended the role of Australian Disability Enterprises such as Flagstaff Group and Greenacres Employment Solutions.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: The Labor member for Kingsford Smith announced support for the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016, which increases one-off compensation payments for eligible supported employees with intellectual disability from 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the difference between their actual wage and the BSWAT productivity-only amount, following the 2015 class action settlement. The speech also highlighted the work of Australian disability enterprises in the electorate, specifically naming Windgap Foundation Limited, and urged the government to quickly implement a new non-discriminatory wage assessment tool.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Amendment Bill 2016 increases payments to eligible supported employees from 50% to 70% of the wage difference under a productivity-only assessment, extends registration deadlines by 12 months, and makes legal advice voluntary to speed up payments. The bill implements a settlement agreement in the Federal Court case *Nojin v Commonwealth* (2012), resolving litigation to provide certainty for Australian Disability Enterprises and their 20,000 workers.
